overlap.title: Complete conquest and continuing inhabitants
overlap.summary: Broad victory summaries in Joshua sit alongside explicit reports that many inhabitants remained.
overlap.reasoning: Joshua itself preserves an exception at Jerusalem, and Judges lists additional unconquered places. Totalizing military language need not mean every settlement was occupied or every person killed. This explicit exception qualifies an unqualified reading of destruction language; it does not by itself establish the historical extent of conquest or resolve the moral assessment of the killings.
overlap.scope: A literal exhaustive reading creates tension; a rhetorical summary of victory allows the stated exceptions. This does not independently date the conquest. Later presence can be explained by incomplete occupation or subsequent return, but these alternatives are not independently demonstrated here. The king list is not a population census or an archaeological chronology. These local accounts may narrate different stages or recap earlier events; their placement alone does not establish a dated sequence.

overlap.title: Faith and works in Romans and James
overlap.summary: Romans rejects justification by works of the law; James rejects faith without action.
overlap.reasoning: The wording is in tension, but the immediate arguments target different problems: reliance on law and an inactive profession of belief.
overlap.scope: Whether these are complementary definitions or divergent emphases is interpretive. The comparison does not establish a scientific claim. These later commendations do not explicitly endorse every statement Rahab made to the pursuers, and reception and action need not be mutually exclusive explanations.

checks.overlapDecision: Distinct house/wall explanation Q beside conquest extent and faith/works records. Retains possible partial fall, house placement and narrative brevity without declaring a contradiction.

overlap.title: A day with delayed sunset
overlap.summary: A literal extra day before sunset departs from ordinary Earth rotation. The account gives no physical mechanism; reading the battle language as poetry changes what is being assessed.
overlap.reasoning: Ordinary apparent daily solar motion is associated with Earth rotation; merely describing the Sun as moving is not the discrepancy. The issue is a literal extension of daylight beyond that cycle, which is not explained by ordinary rotation. The passage cites Jasher and contains elevated battle language, making interpretation relevant.
overlap.scope: This conditional comparison does not show Earth stopped rotating, calculate physical consequences, identify a historical date, or disprove supernatural intervention. NASA supplies the ordinary physical model, not a reconstruction of this battle. A figurative reading does not assert the same physical event.

overlap.title: What was “the book of the wars of the Lord”, and where does its quotation end?
overlap.summary: Numbers cites a written source by name, “the book of the wars of the Lord”, to support a statement about the border at Arnon. No book of that name is among the books of the KJV, the passage does not say who wrote it or when, and the words quoted from it break off without a finished sentence.
overlap.reasoning: The narrative appeals to another writing as its support (“Wherefore it is said in …”), so what that writing was bears on how the book of Numbers describes its own sources. The passage gives a title and a fragment and nothing else: not the author, not the date, not what else the book held. The fragment in the KJV has no main verb of its own after “What he did”, and the passage does not mark where the quotation stops and the narrative resumes.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that it was a collection of war songs or records now lost; that the title is not a title, and the words “war of the Lord” belong to the quotation, as Brenton’s Greek prints them; that the quotation runs through verse 15, or further. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “book of the wars” finds this verse only; Joshua 10:13 is quoted as another place where a narrative cites a named book, not as an answer. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the book was. The difference between the KJV and the Greek wording of the quotation is a separate record; this record concerns the identity and extent of the source named by the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

checks.overlapDecision: Distinct question about Jasher and its quotation boundaries; the published Wars of the Lord Q cites this verse only as context for a different named book. The science record mentions Jasher but does not examine its identity or quotation extent.

overlap.title: The assurance of presence is followed by an apostasy warning
overlap.summary: The chapter promises not to forsake its hearers, then warns of forsaking a people who abandon the covenant.
overlap.reasoning: An unconditional promise for every future circumstance would conflict with the warning. Reading the assurance within covenant loyalty and distinguishing the addressed occasions can reconcile them.
overlap.scope: The condition is supplied by the surrounding warning, not stated in the assurance itself. This does not verify historical divine presence.

overlap.title: A written law is entrusted for custody and periodic public reading
overlap.summary: The narrative attributes law writing to Moses and directs custody beside the ark and a seven-year public reading.
overlap.reasoning: A narrative attribution to Moses is evidence of the authorship claim made within the book, rather than external verification of the surviving book’s complete composition. The closing narrator’s perspective must be distinguished from the earlier law-writing attribution; this distinction alone does not identify an author, editor or date.
overlap.scope: This does not identify the deposited manuscript, establish its survival or show how regularly the reading occurred.

overlap.title: Joshua’s covenant assembly: Shechem or Shiloh?
overlap.summary: The KJV and the Hebrew set Joshua’s last assembly and covenant at Shechem. The Septuagint sets both at Shiloh, before the tent of God, and has no “sanctuary” in verse 26.
overlap.reasoning: The two text traditions name different towns for the same assembly. The Greek place agrees with where Joshua 18:1 puts the tabernacle; the Hebrew and KJV place a “sanctuary of the Lord” at Shechem without saying what it was.
overlap.scope: The passage does not say whether the “sanctuary” at Shechem was the tabernacle, a second holy place or something else, and it mentions no altar there. Do not claim the Greek is a deliberate correction or that the Hebrew is; neither is shown by these editions. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier. English glosses in brackets are the researcher’s plain renderings, not lexicon entries.

checks.overlapDecision: Distinct Q about Joshua’s writing and its book; the custody record does not examine this question and the Shechem/Shiloh G concerns the assembly location.
